newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durables orders tumble in December.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durables orders tumble in December.

text.p: Orders for costly manufactured goods took a surprising tumble in December, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday, suggesting a weaker close for the economy in 1996 than previously thought.

New orders for long-lasting durable goods like new cars and computers dropped 1.7 percent in December to a seasonally adjusted $168.99 billion, sharply contrary to Wall Street economists' forecasts for a pickup in orders.
Shipments of finished manufactured products also weakened in December, and order backlogs were flat.

The December fall was centred in reduced demand for electronic and electrical equipment, specifically communications gear and electronics components, which analysts said made a normally volatile report even harder to interpret.

"It is very confusing and very important," said economist David Orr of First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C., since it goes against anecdotal reports from companies like Intel Corp. of strong markets and potentially hints at less vigour in high-technology industries than realised.

The December fall in total durables orders followed a matching revised 1.7 percent drop in November orders -- the first back-to-back monthly decreases since January and February 1996. Orders were up only a slim 0.6 percent in October, for a generally weak fourth quarter.

Orr said the economy might not have surged as briskly as forecast in the fourth quarter, potentially easing pressure for Federal Reserve policy-makers at a meeting next Tuesday and Wednesday of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee to pre-emptively boost interest rates to dampen inflation pressures.

"Capital spending has been the strongest part of GDP (gross domestic product), but in the fourth quarter, shipments of non-defence capital goods fell at a 5.7 percent annual rate," Orr said. Excluding aircraft, the drop was 2.9 percent.

"Maybe the (anticipated) 4 percent GDP (in the fourth quarter) won't happen," Orr added. The Commerce Department is scheduled to issue its first estimate of the economy's fourth-quarter performance Friday.
The department said that for all of 1996 durable goods orders increased 5.5 percent to $2.03 trillion. Down from a 7.2 percent rise in 1995, it was the weakest gain since a 5.4 percent rise in 1993.
Since the December orders drop was concentrated in the single sector of electronic and electrical machinery, it did not trigger alarm bells about expansion.

"It seems the story with orders right along has been supportive of a moderate growth economy," said William Griggs, managing director of New York bond dealer Griggs & Santow Inc. "This report doesn't change the very moderate uptrend in orders and, in fact, underscores the softness in the economy."
Orders for electronic and electrical equipment plunged 12.5 percent to $24.55 billion in December after a 10.2 percent November increase.
But orders for industrial machinery increased by 1.5 percent to $32.03 billion in December and primary metals gained 2.2 percent to $14.72 billion.

New orders for transportation equipment were flat at $42 billion in December after a 1 percent increase in November. Orders were down for new cars and parts and for aircraft and parts but up for ships, military tanks and railroad equipment.

Aircraft orders also were weak in November, though there are significant orders still in the pipeline. American Airlines has agreed to buy more than $6 billion of airplanes from Boeing Co. But the airline said making the order final was contingent on it reaching a new labour pact with its pilots.

Excluding transportation, durables orders fell last month by 2.2 percent after a big 2.6 percent decline in November. The department said it was the seventh monthly decrease in this category during 1996.

Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indication of business investment in new equipment, were down 0.5 percent in December to $43.69 billion after declining 7.5 percent in November and 0.1 percent in October.
Shipments of durable goods, an indication of current demand, fell 0.8 percent to $168.77 billion after a 0.8 percent rise in November.
Unfilled orders were unchanged in December at $488.91 billion following a 0.3 percent gain in November.
